newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Recent EU decisions on EMU accounting measures.
newsitem.headline: Recent EU decisions on EMU accounting measures.

text.p: European Union governments have used a variety of accounting methods to bring their budget deficits in line with the Maastricht treaty requirements for a single currency.

Following is a list of some of the more controversial decisons, criticised in some quarters as one-off gimmicks, which allow governments to bring their public deficits close to three percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1997.

FRANCE TELECOM - Perhaps the most notorious case involving the transfer of some 37.5 billion French francs from the privatisation of France Telecom to the government's coffers. In November of last year, the EU ruled in favour of the transaction. The deal stipulated that the government would assume the state-owned company's pension liabilities.
ITALIAN EURO TAX - Another one-off measure worth some 5.5 trillion lire, the tax aacounted for roughly 0.19 percent of GDP and was approved by the EU in February.
Many analysts considered the temporary nature of the tax to violate the principle of sustainable budgetary convergence.
GOLD SALES - In line with the Maastricht treaty, gold sales can be used to lower a government's outstanding debt but not its deficit.
Several EU central banks have sold gold in recent months.

INDEX-LINKED GOVERNMENT BONDS -- Two distinct treatments will be applied, depending on whether the bond is linked to a consumer price index, or to a financial asset such as a foreign currency or gold. In the first case, the capital gained or lost due to the movement of the index can be treated as interest and used to reduce a government's deficit.
In the second case, the change in capital cannot be regarded as interest and will have no impact on the deficit.
